utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Just one short information before the continuation of this trial. We have all received health report for Mr. Tadic, and in view of the recommendation of the Detention Unit physician, Mr. Tadic will not be present this afternoon at the trial. I have been made to understand that the Defence of Mr. Zaric will commence in this afternoon with the opening statement, and Mr. Pisarevic advised me that his opening statement will last about one hour and 15 minutes. And if it is completed within that time, I would like to ask you that we don't start with Mr. Tadic without the first witness. That will be only 15 minutes. Because the first witness is Mr. Simeunovic who is extremely important for the defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic and he would like to be present while he is being examined. So tomorrow when we start working normally, there will be no problems for Mr. Tadic to follow the trial when Mr. Simeunovic takes the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber agrees with your proposal, Mr. Lukic, and we shall proceed accordingly. So the Prosecution can continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic. I trust that you're feeling better. If in the course of my questioning, you experience any more difficulties, please ensure that you inform the Chamber straight away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, last week I was asking you some questions regarding the events surrounding the 16th and 17th and 18th of April, and last Thursday you testified that you did not have the impression that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fell that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And you also went on to clarify that you had that impression that had not occurred, then or later. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to some comments provided by Mr. Zaric regarding this issue, and so that you can fully understand his comments, can you please now be shown Exhibit P141 ter. For your information, that is an interview conducted with Mr. Zaric on the 2nd of April, 1998. And in particular, may I ask you to look at page 12 of that interview. Mr. Tadic, the questions that I'm concerned about start about midway down page 12, and the answer continuing on into page 13.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this passage that starts: "Mr. told us"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm referring to the passage where Nancy Paterson, who was asking the questions, is asking Mr. Zaric about a Commander Nikolic receiving a call from Blagoje Simic, informing him that a decision had been made to take over the town. And Mr. Zaric then goes on to provide his answer. And in the course of providing his answer, he points out that Nikolic reported that he had received a phone call from Blagoje Simic during the night of the 16th and 17th. The Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town of Samac, Serbian police and units taking over the vital buildings and objects in the town, and that subsequently the 16th was regarded as a liberation day by the official authorities in the town. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These responses mainly boil down, but I don't know how the response has started. Can you tell me what the first word is? Because I can see here that Mr. -- "Mr. Nikolic told us that he had been informed." Is that at the beginning of the paragraph that you're referring to, or the other one, citing: "You told us that Mr. Nikolic had ordered," or the third one, starting: "You have just told us that Mr. Simic --" I don't know which of the three you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The answer I am primarily interested in you will find on page 13, commencing on the fourth line, that's B/C/S, and you can read that paragraph. Page 13, four lines down.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the part of the third line, saying that on the 17th, in the morning, I don't know exactly for how long, but at any rate, during the night he had been informed by Mr. Simic that the Serbian police forces -- is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's correct. It's that paragraph, that passage. It extends from the third -- fourth line down to about midway in the page. Page 13, that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there they were taking over authority as the Serbian municipality of Samac. If I could only tell to the madam that the official authority, Mr. Simic, and this official authority during the war years, whenever it marked this date, the 16th, I believed that to be the liberation day, you know. I personally do not share this opinion, but they had always emphasised the role of the Serbian police and volunteers, but they never emphasised the 4th Detachment. They did not want to mention that in any case whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, all I'm asking you to do is just read the answer and re-acquaint yourself with it, or acquaint yourself with Mr. Zaric's position. Have you had an opportunity now to read the paragraph? Please inform me when you have. When you have read the paragraph, I will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I proceed reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just -- yes, please read the paragraph and acquaint yourself with the contents.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I wish to say that I had not truly or either it is out of pride, but I'm just saying that that was their entire strategy. They are taking this as the foundation for a new history, but, however, I don't believe it is going to be like this. We have always been, in their eyes, a formation of traitors." Is that as far as you want me to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, there seems to be a communication problem between you and I. I'll repeat. I'll repeat what I want you to do. I just wanted you to read the paragraph in B/C/S on page 13 and acquaint yourself with the content of what Mr. Zaric asserts. You will see the paragraph beginning four lines down on page 13, and it ends midway down page 13. I don't want an answer; I just want an assurance that you have read the paragraph and acquainted yourself with the position that Mr. Zaric adopts. That's all I want you to do. Then I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Di Fazio, you might make it clear to Mr. Tadic whether you want him to read it aloud or read it to himself, because you haven't he said that, you see, so he doesn't know whether he reads it in his mind and becomes acquainted or whether he's supposed to read it out for the record. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Perhaps it will solve the problem by adopting Judge Williams's suggestion. Read it out into the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already read this section. Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You understand what Mr. Zaric is saying in that section?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that answer, Mr. Tadic, Mr. Zaric says that the 4th Detachment, Nikolic, was informed by Blagoje Simic that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town of Samac. Did Mr. Zaric ever inform you that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here at the beginning, I haven't read one sentence which reads: "Mr. Nikolic had told us that he had been informed." I don't know who "we" refers to. Therefore, I do not agree with this plural here, and I was not part of that plural. Because it says that "we had been informed by Mr. Nikolic." That must have been Mr. Zaric and someone else with him. And that is what he told them. Since he didn't tell that to me, I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in that passage, Mr. Zaric makes it clear that he was informed by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town. Did Mr. Zaric ever convey that to you in the days following the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the days, weeks, and months following the 16th and 17th of April, did you, as a member of the Crisis Staff, ever ascertain if the Crisis Staff had participated in the takeover of the town, as Mr. Zaric seems to be aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never learned about this thing, that the Crisis Staff had done something like that, and I wouldn't agree with this statement, because I don't know who the "we" were, in other words, who were informed by Mr. Nikolic. He didn't inform me; therefore, I wasn't involved in this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the course of providing that answer, Mr. Zaric makes it clear that the official authorities in the town regarded the 16th of April as a celebration day, a day of liberation. When was that first celebrated, the 16th and 17th of April? Was it the following year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would only be logical to celebrate the 17th of April, because nothing took place on the 16th. Things happened on the morning of the 17th. However, when it was first celebrated, I don't know. It would only make -- be logical to celebrate the 17th, because the events took place on the morning. And if that was the occasion to celebrate, then that would be on the 17th, in the morning. That's in my view. However, a different decision could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, have you got any idea as to why Mr. Zaric, who was not a member of the Crisis Staff, would be privy to information regarding the Crisis Staff's involvement in a takeover, and you, who were a member of the Crisis Staff, was not privy to any such information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness should first be asked whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff at the time, and then impute to him whether he was aware of that as a member of the Crisis Staff or not. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm well aware that Mr. Tadic was made, on his evidence, a member of the Crisis Staff some five days after the 17th. My question is directed to his having received that information at any time following that. My question is directed to his being able to provide an explanation as to why it was that Mr. Zaric received that information when he was not a member of the Crisis Staff, and he did, when he was a member of the Crisis Staff, notwithstanding the fact that he only became a member of the Crisis Staff five days after the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to be clear about: This information from the interview which Mr. Zaric was given, is the implication that it was given -- he was told some days after the 17th? MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Zaric is saying in the interview that he was informed by Nikolic of the participation of the Crisis Staff in the takeover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: He received that information. He was not a member of the Crisis Staff. Mr. Tadic has never received any such information and is unaware of Crisis Staff participation in the takeover. My question is directed to ascertaining if Mr. Tadic can explain why it is that Mr. Zaric received the information, even though he's not a member of the Crisis Staff, and Mr. Tadic has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: You understand my question, don't you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I fully understand the question. First of all, we are speaking here about Mr. Zaric and Mr. Nikolic and some other people who knew -- who had this information. I presume that Mr. Zaric, given the fact that he was a security officer or, in other words, he was involved in security issues, he in any case had more broader interests in that respect than I had. At the time that we are discussing, and that is the 16th and 17th of April, I wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff, and I knew nothing about these activities. How Zaric came to have this kind of information, I really wouldn't be able to say. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the interview. I'd like the witness now to be shown, please, Exhibit P21. Again, Mr. Tadic, would you acquaint yourself with the document. When I say "acquaint," what I mean is read it, have a look at it, understand what the contents are so that I may then question you about it. That's what I mean by acquainting yourself with the document. Mr. Tadic, now I'll ask you some questions about the document, now that you've had an opportunity to acquaint yourself with it. That's a report of the 17th Corps command, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And it's a report of the 17th Corps command; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a report -- at least, that's what's written here by the 17th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The first sentence refers to a takeover of all vital facilities in Bosanski Samac during the night of the 16th and 17th. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Midway through the second and large paragraph, it refers to forces of Tactical Group 17, units of the Serb Territorial Defence and the police participating in actions during the takeover of vital facilities in Bosanski Samac. Do you see that sentence, midway through the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, the forces of the 17th Tactical Group took part, the Serbian TO, on the police force. Are you referring to the passage where it says also that the situation is calm now in the town, the attack had been repelled and the enemy suffered losses in the operation of taking over the vital facilities in the town, forces of the 17th Tactical Group, the Serbian police, and the TO took part, and the situation in the town now is calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right. Now, the forces of Tactical Group 17 that participated in this takeover of vital facilities on the night of the 16th and 17th were the 4th Detachment, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some time ago, I already said that the 17th Tactical Group forces -- I didn't say particularly this, but I did say that the 17th Tactical Group forces had many units. However, here it does not say explicitly that this was the 4th Detachment. I fully agree with this report, and I believe, without knowing about it, I imparted the information that I had and formulated them in particular this way, that the town had been taken by these forces. You have to ask whether the 4th Detachment was part of the 17th Tactical Group. You have to ask the author of this report. I do not deny that the 17th Tactical Group was also the 4th Detachment, but it does not say like that in this report. It just refers to the 17th Tactical Group, and it could be the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, or the 4th Detachment or any other detachment. I didn't know who the 17th Tactical Group belonged to. We spoke last year -- last week about this armoured vehicle, and I mentioned that it was there but that it did not belong to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you see if you can possibly answer my next questions with a yes or a no, if you can, of course. The 4th Detachment was part of the 17th Tactical Group; correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The primary area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment included Bosanski Samac; correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This document clearly establishes that forces of the 17th Tactical Group operated, along with Serbian police, on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992; correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you saying that the military formation or unit that was primarily responsible for Bosanski Samac that was part of the 17th Tactical Group was not the unit -- the forces of the Tactical Group referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only disputable thing here is which units of the 17th Tactical Group took part. Nothing else is disputable. So if the author of this report had put the 1st detachment, the 2nd or the 3th or the 4th Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group or a motorised unit, then this document would be much more clear. However, I think that by referring to this 17th Tactical Group, it means that it comprised a large number of detachment. For instance, this armoured vehicle, for instance, if we omit everything else, was not part of the 4th Detachment, if we put everything else aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you're informed, as assistant commander of logistics in the 4th Detachment, of the activities or operations of any other elements in the 17th Tactical Group on the night of the 16th and 17th of April? Other elements, by that I mean other than the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, isn't it the case that you know well that the forces of Tactical Group 17 that participated in the 16th and 17th of April takeover of vital facilities in Bosanski Samac -- there's a reference, in fact, to the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment is mentioned, because it belongs to the 17th Tactical Group. It's not expressly mentioned -- the 4th Detachment is not expressly mentioned, but the 17th Tactical Group is mentioned, so I am including that into the 17th Tactical Group, as well as some other detachments that were a part of it. We cannot claim here that it was the 4th Detachment, just as I'm not claiming that it was not a part of the 17th Tactical Group, even though this is a purely military question and I'm only interpreting this as a person who has it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to remind you of some other evidence that you provided to the Chamber last Friday, the -- on Friday, the 14th of February. For the benefit of Defence counsel, they will find this in LiveNote at page 53. In providing answers to your counsel, Mr. Lukic, you discussed the arrival of paramilitaries at Batkusa, and you made the following points, and I'll quote the evidence to you later if you disagree, but however, I'll summarise what I have read from the transcript. You made the point that everyone knew that the paramilitaries had arrived from Serbia in JNA helicopters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You made the point that their arrival was discussed at 4th Detachment headquarters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You made the point that this discussion was in the context of an informal meeting. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you were informed by the commander that these paramilitaries would have no contact with the 4th Detachment. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Therefore, the 4th Detachment commander had been provided with information as to the movements of the paramilitaries. That follows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be like that, but I don't know about any such information. He could have known about that information, just as I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is a little unclear what the Prosecutor means by the movements of the paramilitaries. Perhaps this could be clarified. Because to me it is not clear what the Prosecutor means. Which period is he thinking of about the paramilitaries? He's talking about the 4th Detachment, knowledge about it, and then he's talking about the movement of the paramilitaries. So I don't know what he means by this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the witness obviously hasn't experienced any difficulties. He was able to answer the questions with simple yes or no answers. But for Mr. Lukic's point of view, if Your Honour pleases, the passage I'm referring to is on page 53, and Mr. Tadic said this: "I don't think it was an official meeting. We were just told that they had arrived. And I think that the commander said that they will not be coming to Samac and that they will not have any contact with the 4th Detachment." Not coming to Samac, number 2, will not have contact with the 4th Detachment. It's the provision of that information to Mr. Tadic and other members of the 4th Detachment at this informal meeting that I am concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It would seem that the people who were providing information knew the role of the special forces. Perhaps that's what you are trying to find out. MR. DI FAZIO: That's exactly my question. I hope that explains it for Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any problems with that if the word "movement" means their arrival to Samac. So this is what I wanted the Prosecutor to clarify, the movement. Does he mean when they arrived to the municipality or does he mean the 16th or the 17th? MR. DI FAZIO: Solve the problem by substituting the word "activities" instead of "movements." Would that be better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be clearer. MR. DI FAZIO: We'll do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, it follows as a matter of logic that the commander of the 4th Detachment who informed you that the paramilitaries would not be coming to Samac and who informed you that the paramilitaries would not have contact with the 4th Detachment had information as to the intended activities of the paramilitaries; that is so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask him. I don't know what he had amongst his papers or in his head. He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is pure speculation. It's guessing about what the commander could have known, what his information was about those activities. So that would be his knowledge about the commander. So it's pure speculation. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not speculation about what the commander knows. It's anything but speculation. Mr. Tadic's evidence is clear. The commander of the 4th Detachment told him and other assembled members of the 4th Detachment what was going to be happening. They would not be coming to Samac and they wouldn't have contact. How does he know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not in dispute. Tadic said that. But not what the commander knew, but what he told Tadic. The question is what did the commander know about those people. But Tadic's reply was what the commander told him. So a question could be: What does Tadic think that the commander knew? And this is pure speculation, and this is what the Prosecutor is asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell that to me. He said that as a comment. He didn't say: Mr. Tadic such-and-such. But he just made a comment that they would not be coming to Samac, and then he went on to say the other things. I don't know what he meant by that. I don't know if he had any wider instructions. He didn't inform us about that at the time. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution's questions are quite clear, Mr. Tadic, so I think it's better to give straightforward answers. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't intend to press for an answer. He's provided, I think, an answer already to a previous questions before Mr. Lukic stood up, and in any event, I'm satisfied with the answers that I've obtained, unless the Chamber wishes me to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tadic. That's all I want to ask you about the events of the 16th and 17th of April. I'd now like to turn to another topic, and that is Crisis Staff membership. I would just like you to re-establish for the Trial Chamber who was a member of the Crisis Staff and who was not, and their areas of expertise. First of all, we know that Blagoje Simic was president of the Crisis Staff and that he was a member of the SDS, president of the local SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje was the president of the Crisis Staff. Whether he was that as part -- as a president of the SDS, I don't know. I think for a while that he wasn't a president of the SDS. So I don't know when he became president, and I don't know those relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mitar Mitrovic was the secretary of the Crisis Staff and a member of the Crisis Staff, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a secretary, secretary of the Crisis Staff. I think that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I never quite clarified that. But he was always present, and an observer who didn't see any of the documents could conclude that he was also a member of the Crisis Staff, because he was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were, of course, a member, and your area of responsibility was civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. I was in charge of civilian protection first, and then I was a member of the Crisis Staff, and not a member of the Crisis Staff in charge of civilian protection. So it's the other way around. First I was the commander of the civilian protection and then after that I became a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Milos Bogdanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff. His area of responsibility was as chief of the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also thought that he was a member of the Crisis Staff, but -- and that he had the post that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff by virtue of his position as chief of the Secretariat of National Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, it's more than just possible, is it not? Let me quote to you from P138, P138 ter, page 50. I don't think you need to be shown it, because I'll just read it out. It's only two lines. You were being asked questions by Nancy Paterson..

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So was Mr. Bogdanovic a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because of his post as chief of Secretariat of the National Defence, he had to be a member of the Crisis Staff. That position is very, very clear, isn't it, the position that you adopted in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio, but Mr. Tadic already did answer that on -- here, page 17. Your question, line 8, Mr. Tadic's answer line 11, where he said that Mr. Bogdanovic had the post that you have mentioned. But then you asked the question again, and that's where Mr. Tadic gave what you thought was a more I think ambiguous answer. But he had quite clearly answered straightforwardly on lines 11 and 12. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If that is so, does it not mean that Mr. Bozo Ninkovic also became a member of the Crisis Staff upon his appointment as chief of Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Bozo Ninkovic was appointed chief of the Secretariat when the Crisis Staff had already stopped operating, once it became the War Presidency. I'm not sure about the dates, but I think that he became the chief when the Crisis Staff had stopped operating and when the War Presidency had started to function. And I think that Bozo Ninkovic was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I don't have any reason to think otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic and later Milan Simic were also members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about Mirko Jovanovic that I assumed that he was a member of the Crisis Staff because he had the main word there. As far as Milan Simic is concerned, he came there sometime in early June, I think, instead of Mirko Jovanovic, and I said that I thought that Mr. Milan Simic was not a member of the Crisis Staff. That was my impression, because he appeared less frequently. And then when he did come, he talked about finances and the situation with the Executive Board and so on. I don't have any other information. I don't think that anyone said that Mr. Milan Simic again is a member of the Crisis Staff or that any kind of solution was made. He was there very briefly because the Crisis Staff then later transformed and became the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Simeon Simic was on the Crisis Staff and his area of expertise or responsibility was information services, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, yes. I knew Simeon Simic well, and I think that that's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Todorovic was obviously a member, and his area of responsibility was the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the way he behaved, the impression could have been formed that that was so. However, according to his function, just as the others were part of the civilian authority, I can claim that according to his function, he could not have been a member of the Crisis Staff, even though I didn't attach much importance to that at the time. But he did appear frequently, and in the way he behaved, he seemed to be a very important person at such meetings. He always wished to be the person who had the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And Fadil Topcagic, he was a member of the 4th Detachment, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Fadil Topcagic was a member of the 4th Detachment. I heard that he was a member of the Crisis Staff, but I never saw him at a meeting. He was never there when I was there. I don't know if he was there at other times when I wasn't there. That's something that I don't know. But he was never at a meeting of the Crisis Staff at the same time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was his area of responsibility, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were never at a meeting of the Crisis Staff together, or that he said anything there, my conclusion is that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your position on the Crisis Staff was linked to your appointment as chief of civilian protection, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You kept that position throughout all of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At some point during 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question is not clear, because the way it was interpreted, this last question, line -- page 20, line 10: "You kept that position," while before he mentioned the position in the Crisis Staff and the position in the civilian protection. So which post does he mean when he says: "You kept that position throughout all of 1992," whether the one of the membership in the Crisis Staff or the one in the civilian protection? Because he mentioned both posts in the question before. MR. DI FAZIO: I was referring to Mr. Tadic's role in the civilian protection. I think he understood that to be that way. I'll ask it again just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you understood, didn't you, when you said that you kept your post throughout 1992, that you were talking about your post as chief of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your post on the Crisis Staff stopped when the Crisis Staff ceased to exist and the War Presidency took over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was in accordance with superior orders. I don't know whether it was the Assembly or somebody else decided that reorganisation needed to be carried out, and it was carried out, and the staff of the civilian protection returned to a kind of normal situation. So that it was a part of the Secretariat for National Defence, like it was before. So only for a short period in certain conditions was it separated, more in the way of location rather than in an organisational sense. So it was moved from the staff, from the Secretariat for National Defence. Later it was returned to the staff, to the Secretariat for National Defence, and that's where it is still functioning today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who else lost their position as a result of the change of name from Crisis Staff to War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who were not in accordance with the law that was adopted at the time, or the regulation. All of those that were not included in that regulation or that law. I don't know what it was. But whatever it was that caused the change to come about, either regulation or the law. So if something else, something new is formed, it's formed on the basis of a specific regulation or a law. So all of those who do not fit in with that regulation or that law are no longer members. So it's reorganisation under certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The situation that the Crisis Staff faced in 1992 was one of considerable stress, wasn't it? There was a state of emergency declared, wartime conditions existed, war damage had been sustained to the municipality and the town, resources were low. You'd agree with that general picture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It was very -- a very delicate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was responsible for the provision of essential services, for example, water, electricity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It was responsible for repair of war damage, provision of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was carried out by certain services, mostly repair. I don't know what you consider to be war damage, but if you're thinking of damage to buildings and so on, it's not something that was done by the staff, but it was carried out by specific services, and those services were initially linked with the civilian protection staff, and then later to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It was responsible for housing, the provision of information to the people, security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were services that were in charge of accommodation also. We've heard that here. Initially, the services of the Executive Board and then later the secretariat that was formed was in charge of that, and people who testified explained that here, clearly. They were the ones who dealt with accommodation, and there was a separate, special group for humanitarian aid. That was the Red Cross and the Department for Social Work, as it was called. They were the ones mostly who carried out those tasks. It couldn't be said that the Crisis Staff was in charge of accommodation. That really would not be an appropriate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But it was in charge of information and security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it would be informing or what kind of security it would be in charge of. As far as I'm concerned, I did not attend any meetings to that effect, so I don't know perhaps if a report had to be sent higher. Perhaps the informing would then be done to this effect or in this aspect. The protection would be something that the civilian police would be in charge of, and military security would be in the hands of the military police of a specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was imperative that the Crisis Staff be kept informed of developments in all of those areas that I've just mentioned to you, by its members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, everybody had their own line of reporting, and everybody, in accordance with their own line, provided this information. For example, a large number of information was sent to the Executive Board, and then the Executive Board would be informing the Crisis Staff. Not every single service went -- small service went to the Crisis Staff. I said that they were related to the Executive Board, and the Executive Board would summarise all of that and submit it or inform the Crisis Staff. But I'm not saying that sometimes some service would come to discuss its problems separately before the Crisis Staff. As far as security was concerned, that had its own line and possibly Todorovic would be somebody at the Crisis Staff who could say something about security, but this was unofficial. While military security did not have any contact with the Crisis Staff. That is more or less my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said in your interview, P138 ter, at page 51, that you went to Crisis Staff sessions and "important matters in my domain were discussed." So you provided reports of matters for which you were responsible to the Crisis Staff. I don't want a disposition on everything that you did, but just yes or no: Did you provide reports on your area of responsibility to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In specific situations I informed the Crisis Staff if that was necessary, but only about, so to say, major issues that would be of interest for the Crisis Staff. Of course, I don't inform them that I needed, for example, ten litres of fuel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I understand and I think the Trial Chamber understands. Also in your interview at P138 ter, page 54, you said that other civilians provided reports on specialist areas, such as flood protection, electricity supply, reports from the director of the medical centre. Do you recall saying that in your interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In certain situations, when that extended the scope of minor problem, people would come to the Crisis Staff and inform it on the situation in their respective domains. That was particularly the case concerning the situation with medicaments, especially for dialysis, which was difficult to overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you recall during the course of your examination-in-chief that you said that the -- that votes, casting of votes in the Crisis Staff, rarely occurred because consensus was reached through discussion? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you recall your counsel, Mr. Lukic, putting to Mr. Todorovic many months ago that the Crisis Staff assisted you in a hands-on sort of way, for example, by helping with the arrangement of funerals, and Mr. Todorovic agreed? Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that evidence, and that was not the case. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I'll return to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you said in your interview, P138 ter, page 55, that the Crisis Staff issued instructions to you in a global sense, and I use your words. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what is written, then it's correct, but that was a long time ago for me to remember each and every sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of course. If you wish, I'll put it to you. Do you want me to read the passage to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if that's what is written, I agree that that's what I said. But as I said, it's difficult to remember every sentence that I ever uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of course. I understand that. And if you want me to put these quotes to you, I'm more than happy to. Would you agree, as a matter of fact, regardless of what you said in the interviews, that the Crisis Staff issued instructions to you in a global sense?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the situation is one where members of the Crisis Staff report on their activities to the Crisis Staff, discussion occurs within the Crisis Staff, voting is unnecessary because -- or rarely occurs because consensus is reached through discussion, specialist reports are provided to the Crisis Staff, there's a full and frank discussion of issues of concern to the Crisis Staff within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with your last part of the statement, that there was frank discussion or any -- I don't know which kind of discussion you meant. There was no love lost, as one may deduce from what you said. There were discussions. Some of them were heated discussions and difficult ones and unbearable ones, et cetera, but we managed -- it was possible to find always the way out of the situation. However, one cannot speak of any love lost in any part of their activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought that's exactly what the Prosecution meant when he said that these were frank discussions, because some of them were heated, as you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree with you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And so therefore, the Crisis Staff was kept informed of major developments in the community for which it was responsible, such as the numbers of people being exchanged, the prisons and detention camps being set up, the leading figures around the town who were being arrested, the torture and beatings that were being conducted in the prisons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the above.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You agree, don't you, that the fact of incarceration of non-Serbs, mass arrests, was something that was widely known in the community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One may say that that was common knowledge, but a minute ago you said that I had specific relations with the Crisis Staff and that I was receiving, so to say, global instructions from that. After that, you listed all that of which I have -- over which I had no jurisdiction and with which I had no connections. It would only be fair if you mentioned just the activities that I performed and for which I had the consent -- I had an agreement with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've agreed that the phenomenon of mass arrest of non-Serbs was common knowledge. Was the torture and beating of non-Serbs who had been arrested also a matter of common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't say that everybody knew, but quite a few people did know. There were only 200 policemen, just to mention that. And if you had all those people knowing that, so that was quite a figure. And from these men, other people could have learned what was happening, so one can conclude that a large number of people was aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is it not the case, Mr. Tadic, that the Crisis Staff, as a body, was aware of these mass arrests of non-Serbs and the torture and beating of the prisoners in the detention camps set up in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that I had some knowledge of that, and I already told you what the reactions were to this knowledge of mine and possible interventions. The same case was with the rest. I do not claim that the Crisis Staff, as an organ, was informed of this -- of any of this directly or by the people who worked there. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P128 ID, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. While the exhibit is being found: You asked Mr. Tadic, on page 25, lines -- 24 and 25, concerning himself and the Crisis Staff, and you asked him whether the Crisis Staff had issued instructions in a global sense. Mr. Tadic replied yes. And then later on we have this reference to global instructions. I really am not that certain that I understand what a global instruction is in the context of what we're talking about, so I wonder whether you could clarify it, because you yourself, Mr. Di Fazio, were the one who raised the terminology. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll clarify it, if Your Honour pleases, by taking Mr. Tadic to the precise words he used, and then we can invite some comment on that. Perhaps the witness can be shown P138 [Realtime transcript read in error "128"] ter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could you confirm whether it is P128 or P138 because it comes across as 138, but the transcript reflects 128. MR. DI FAZIO: P138 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think for the assistance of the registry assistant, Mr. Di Fazio had asked for P128, and then I intervened with my question, and now -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And now he's asking for a second document with respect to these global instructions. MR. DI FAZIO: I will return to P128, but later after I've dealt with this issue. And can the witness now be shown P138.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but can I be excused for five minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that we can take our break now and then -- it's almost 10.15. Then we continue at a quarter to 11.00. So we shall take an early break and continue at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution continues. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I wonder if Exhibit P138 could be given to -- 138 ter could be given to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you just read your answers. The passage I'm particularly interested in commences at the bottom of page 55. However, you will see that it's preceded by a question from Nancy Paterson. You can read that halfway through page 55. She was asking you if you were basically taking your orders or given instructions by the Crisis Staff. And then you provide your answer, and your answer commences at the bottom of page 55 and continues over the page into page 56.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, and it begins with "globally." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Globally, yes, because we worked on a case-by-case basis, because we had to solve very often vital problems for the civilian population living in Samac. We established a series of various social workers teams assigned with specific tasks. If, for example, a shell demolished somebody's house, and if that could be mended quickly, meaning that it was not completely devastated, then a team would immediately go there afterwards -- after the shelling to repair it. If somebody's windows were broken, such person would come and report that his windows had been broken by a shell, and then a team would go over there, entrusted with the job of glazing. At the beginning, we did the glazing at a large scale; however, very soon we realised that that was a useless job, because today we would put the windows on and the next day they would be destroyed. So Therefore, we decided to put plastic foils, and it happened that after a certain time, almost all houses had plastic foils on the windows in Samac. Then there were various different teams helping the civilian population at that time, et cetera. Is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Thank you very much. Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the question and the answer, on page 30, line 4, Mr. Tadic in fact did not read it correctly, and he said -- where he said: Frequent vital problems. Whereas in the document it says purely vital problems. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, I'm not asking you about broken glass or anything like that, or replacement of windows. What I'd like you to do is explain to the Chamber, and this follows from the question from Her Honour, Judge Williams, what you meant when you said that in a global sense, globally, on a case-by-case basis, you took instructions from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, globally, for example, if some 30 houses were demolished in Samac, and if I said on the Crisis Staff that we had some 30 houses, I didn't refer to individual cases of this and this individual, but I rather said globally that some 30 houses had been demolished that need to be repaired, and that was that. So there were no particular and specific information about the extent of the damage, the name of the house, and things like that. Or if I spoke about the need for the raw material for building caskets, coffins, then I would say that we need this kind of material, without saying for whom it was intended. I just said that we need a big quantity of the material, and then they would tell me: "You should refer this issue to the Executive Board for them to procure this material." If there was a case of exchange, I would just say that an exchange took place on the 6th or 7th July, 1992, in which 200 people were exchanged. And that was a global information. I didn't give them the list or read out the list of the names of the people who were exchanged. This was the global information that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you provided the Crisis Staff with the big picture, so to speak, of your activities

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As did other members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others, not only members of the Crisis Staff, like the ones whom I mentioned, for example, if the seeding operation had to be done, for example, somebody would say that we had planned to sow 1.500 hectares and then they would say: "You should refer the particulars to the Executive Board, who would provide the seed for you." So in my modest view, these were the global issues that were not elaborated in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I take that answer to be agreement that other members of the Crisis Staff provided the Crisis Staff with reports of the big picture insofar as their areas of responsibility were concerned? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, more or less like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just move very briefly into private session, if Your Honour pleases? There's one brief matter that I need to attend to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, again, if you can possibly answer questions with a yes or a no, I would appreciate it. You took the performance of your duties at the Crisis Staff seriously, very seriously?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within my domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You did your best to perform your duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You did your best to assist the Crisis Staff to carry out its functions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that domain, I didn't do very much. I did whatever was possible within my domain, or even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were carrying out duties assigned to you by the Crisis Staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that, because it wasn't the Crisis Staff who told me to repair the houses, to bury people, to take care of shutting off the water for it not to be frozen. These things were not ordered to me by the Crisis Staff, because that was not within their jurisdiction. There were just current affairs that derived or were dictated by certain situation that the Crisis Staff wasn't aware of at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your good performance in civilian protection assisted the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My good performance was in the form of assistance in establishing, so to say, normal conditions in the town where we lived. In other words, to assist the population for them to feel as much possibly normally as they can under the given circumstances. I never gave it a thought what the Crisis Staff would think about my work. I was more interested in how the people were going to survive under the circumstances in which I was trying to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you actively working against the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did my job, and I didn't do anything against the Crisis Staff, because I didn't think it was against the interest of the Crisis Staff if one helped the situation -- the population. So helping the people was not against the interests of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As a member of the Crisis Staff, was it not your duty to assist it to perform its functions in whatever way you could, whatever way was asked of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the domain of my responsibility, I did it in a correct way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You do not agree with or support the discrimination by one ethnic group against other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were the policies of the Crisis Staff of which you were a member discriminatory in any way, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't feel that at any given moment in time. From all the documents, it could be discerned, and also through the actions, that this did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 16th of April, 1992, there was in existence a democratically elected Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It countered in its membership Croats, Muslims, and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, it no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what form it existed, because at the time I did not have any contacts with that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you telling this Chamber that you don't know, that you don't know if the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac had ceased to exist on the 17th and 18th and 19th of April? Is that the position, your position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I don't know in which form it was in those days, in relation to the 16th, because a number of deputies, as we have heard here, continued to work. I wasn't a deputy. I wasn't in the Assembly, so I didn't really have any insight into all of that. The form that it had on the 16th was not maintained on the 17th. But I don't know what this form was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The situation is, is it not, that it was dead, defunct, moribund, finished, and you knew that well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that it was moribund. I would just say that it didn't function. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P89.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you're aware, aren't you, that the municipality of Bosanski Samac -- just before we get on to this document: The municipality of Bosanski Samac, the one that existed on the 16th of April, 1992, had been democratically elected earlier, in 1991, I believe? Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I did hear more or less what it's about. Before the 16th, there was this democratically elected municipality, the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at P89. That is the decision on the introduction of a state of emergency. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in Article 2, it sweeps away the existing institutions, including the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All bodies of the institution of the municipality of Bosanski Samac will cease to function in their present composition, and all of their functions, rights, and duties are taken over by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to object to this line of questioning. If maybe Mr. Tadic is a legal or constitutional expert, he can given his answers, but otherwise I don't see the justification of this line of questioning, since we saw in the previous proceedings that he is neither military expert nor I believe he's a legal expert and we are entering into the area of legal issues. So maybe my learned friend can rephrase the question, or maybe establish the foundation why he's asking the answers from this witness, who is obviously not a legal expert. That's the basis of my objection. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I would have thought that the introduction of a state of emergency, a document that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting for the interpretation to end. Mr. Pantelic, I think your objection is misconceived. The witness is being asked on the contents of the document before him. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So Article 2 essentially sweeps away --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, and to my learned friend. And the other fact, undisputed fact, is that Mr. Tadic was not a member of Crisis Staff at the period when this document was issued, so I believe that it's well out of scope of his -- MR. DI FAZIO: I know that, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, there's no problem at all with the line of questioning that the Prosecution has embarked on. There is a document before the witness and he's simply asking him about the contents which the witness is reading. So please do sit down. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, please don't read it out. Please don't provide a commentary. Please, if you can, answer with a simple yes or no. Article 2 sweeps away those bodies that had made up the municipality, and in particular, the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the democratically elected municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it states here. But this doesn't look to me like a document, like a usual document from the Crisis Staff, like the ones I could see later and then it says who the document is delivered to, to the files, to the Crisis Staff. On the left side it should state whom the document is given to, and also whom the copies should be distributed to. This to me looks like it was done pretty quickly, in a haste. So I don't know anything about this document. I can just confirm what it states in the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But you can confirm, can't you, that on the 17th and thereafter, to this day, the municipality of Bosanski Samac never operated again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that as of this date, until today, two municipalities of Bosanski Samac functioned. One is Bosanski Samac Domaljevac and the other is Samac. That's what I know. So at that time, the same paper like this one was introduced at the Domaljevac Samac municipality, where the majority population were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you saying that the municipality of Bosanski Samac decided to dismember itself and set itself up as two separate institutions, one in Domaljevac and one in the town of Bosanski Samac? Is that what you're telling the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the Prosecutor's question. Could you please repeat the question. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you saying that the municipality of Bosanski Samac decided to dismember itself and set itself up as two separate institutions, one in Domaljevac and one in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what agreement they reached, but in any case, there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is it not the case, very simple proposition that I put to you, that on the 16th of April, a democratically elected municipality of Bosanski Samac existed, it never existed again from the 17th onwards in that form? You would agree with that, at least, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you do not agree with me that as of that point, there were two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you aware of any decision that you can point to or any document, any evidence of deliberations carried out by the municipality of Bosanski Samac on or before the 16th of April, where it decided to set itself up as a Serbian municipality in Bosanski Samac and another municipality in Domaljevac? Are you aware of that matter ever being discussed or aired?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate at the municipality meetings, so I don't know whether they discussed that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. If you continue to look at P89, Article 3 establishes that the Crisis Staff is responsible for taking over all duties and tasks of the Bosanski Samac municipality. Do you see that in Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that is in fact what happened: The Crisis Staff took over the duties and functions of the municipality that had existed on the 16th? I'm sorry. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard what you stated, and that's what it says here. Yes. You noted that -- and I don't have any comment on that. If that's what it says, then what you said is correct, if that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to go a bit further, though. It's not just what the document says; it's in fact what happened and what you saw. The Crisis Staff of the municipality carried out the duties and tasks that had previously been carried out by the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff continued to perform certain tasks, to carry out certain tasks. Whether those were the same ones that were carried out by the Assembly or whether they were broader or narrower, I would not be able to say, because I do not know much about the work of the Assembly. It continued -- it carried out certain tasks. Whether they were the same tasks as those of the municipality or whether that was somewhat modified, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff was carrying out the functions of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac until such time as that municipality could meet, that Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was carried out by the Crisis Staff initially. Then it was done by the War Presidency, and then, when the conditions were possible, a municipality -- Assembly was formed, as you were able to hear in this Chamber from those who are much better informed about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P124.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That is the gazette. It's been referred to often in the proceedings, Mr. Tadic, and I'll take you to various portions of it. Can you please look at Article 1, very briefly, and again if you can possibly answer with a yes or a no, I would appreciate it. The Article 1 makes it clear that this Municipal Assembly, which is founded, is one of Serbian people and does not refer to the other two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, in the beginning I said that I'm a professor of mechanical engineering, so I can only read this gazette or any other, because I am literate enough to be able to do that. So as far as interpretations of the gazette, I would kindly ask you not to seek such an opinion from me, because I'm sure there are more competent people who can tell you about that. I can read it out and I can state that yes, that is what it says there, but about the meaning or interpretations, I really would not be able to tell you anything about that. If you consider this something important, I can read it and I can give you my interpretation of it, but I don't think that that would be anything important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm not seeking your interpretation or legal opinion; I'm simply asking you this: When you read Article 1, it establishes a Municipal Assembly of Serbian people? You don't need to be a lawyer to read that sentence, do you? And that's what it says, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you've read it out, yes, that's what it states there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And Article 5. Go to Article 5. That simply says that this Assembly is only going to have members who are deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, or members of Serbian ethnicity. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that that article states that deputies of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo, in the process of being established, as well as other deputies among the ranks of the Serbian people following the signing of a statement of joining this Assembly, and that's what it states here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the gazette says that the Crisis Staff, and you will find this in Article 1 under paragraph 5 -- I'm afraid I don't know where in the B/C/S it appears. I believe it's page 8 of the B/C/S version. Page 8. If Your Honours please, it's page 14 of the English translation. Under Article 1, second paragraph, it says that the municipal Crisis Staff is to be composed of representatives of political, military, and other institutions of Serbian people. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes. It's on line 2 of Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The result of all of that is the complete disenfranchisement of Croats and Muslims in the community.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, I know it's my opinion. I'm asking you: Is the result of all of those provisions the complete disenfranchisement of Croats and Muslims in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what they were allowed to vote for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that there was no voting for anyone at that time, there was no voting for them either. Nobody voted for anything. Had there been any voting, they would also have been able to come out and vote for anything, and this is what happened later, when there was a vote in later years. Everybody came out to vote: Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. And that's what it was like in Samac also. And the Assembly of Republika Srpska had representatives of the Muslim, Croat, and Serb people when the voting was carried out, and it is like that to this very day. The Samac Municipal Assembly to this day, whenever there is voting, has representatives of the Serbian, the Muslim, and the Croat people voted in. I don't know the exact number, but there is a large number of deputies of Croat or Muslim ethnicity, and most of them are Serbs. But when a vote is conducted, everybody has the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm not asking you about the current situation; I'm asking you about the situation as it existed in 1992 and 1993. The result of those provisions that I've directed your attention to is the complete disenfranchisement of Croats and Muslims; they're not allowed to have their representatives; only Serbs are allowed to be members of this body. That is plain; you accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is clear, there is nothing there to accept or not to accept, if that is clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is clear --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the Assembly, and I don't know what its composition was. I don't know whether it had other deputies. And I know how it was when voting was carried out. At that time, there was no voting. But I know how it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were, however, in the Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff was the manifestation of the Municipal Assembly until such time as the Municipal Assembly, the Serbian Municipal Assembly, could function. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. If I'm not mistaken, you claim that Fadil Topcagic also was a member of the Crisis Staff, even though I say that I never attended any meetings with him, but that does not mean that he was not a member. But Fadil, according to everything that I know, is not a Serb, so ....

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you agree that to deprive ethnic peoples of their representatives in a legislative body is discriminatory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying to you now that at that time there was discrimination towards all. At that time, I didn't vote for anything. I didn't vote for the Crisis Staff, nor for the War Presidency, or for - I don't know - deputies. Nobody voted for anything then. So why would there be discrimination against some and no discrimination against others? Nobody had any rights as far as voting was concerned, because there was no voting. We can talk about discrimination during the period when voting is carried out. If there was a vote in 1992 and Muslims and Croats did not vote, then that is discriminatory. But if there was no voting, then there is no discrimination. I would not really want to come out with any legal theories here, because that is something that I'm really not that well informed about. But anyway, this is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I don't seek an explanation of what voting took place, where and when. My question is simple: Do you agree that to deprive ethnic peoples of their representatives in a legislative body is discriminatory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just explained to you what I think. I still stand by that and I still think that that is so. Please understand: I didn't move in those circles. I wasn't in those assemblies. So it is difficult for me now to speak to you about that in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you aware of how the Croats and Muslims felt in Bosanski Samac when they no longer had their political representatives in the old municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know how they felt? No one complained to me, no one from them, to say: "Well, I don't have my own representative. And this is something that is affecting me." Nobody complained in those terms. None of the Muslims complained to me either, even though I had contacts with very many Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is it the case from everything that you have just said in the last few minutes in answer to these questions, agreement by you that to deprive two ethnic groups of their political representatives is discriminatory? Just tell us yes or no. If you can possibly answer that question is a yes or no, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with such an assumption that there is discrimination against anyone along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you be happy to be a member of a body that disenfranchises ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. How do you mean, to be a member of a body?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you function within any organ or body that is effectively discriminating against ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not work in such a body.
